extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students (introductory proofs / real analysis / set theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Worked solutions and method patterns for problems in elementary proofs, functions, limits, sequences, and countability (from Richard Hammack's Book of Proof). Shows standard proof templates and constructive bijections used in undergraduate coursework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show a function is bijective
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a function f : A → B is bijective, demonstrate that it is both injective and surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Injective: assume f(m)=f(n) and deduce m=n (example: f(n)=2^n, take log2). Surjective: for arbitrary b∈B produce an a∈A with f(a)=b (example: if B consists of powers of 2, write b=2^n and use n). Combine injective and surjective proofs to conclude bijectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find inverse of a bijection by solving f(x)=y
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute f^{-1} by expressing y = f(x) and algebraically solving for x in terms of y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: f(n)=2^n ⇒ f^{-1}(n)=log_2(n); f(x)=πx−e ⇒ f^{-1}(x)=(x+e)/π. For multivariable maps, solve the system for input coordinates (see f((x,y)) = ((x^2+1)y, x^3) and solving for x,y in terms of outputs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove injectivity for functions on product domains
rubrics_metrics.description: When domain is A×B and codomain pairs, equate output coordinates and deduce equality of input coordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set f(a1,b1)=f(a2,b2) to get componentwise equalities; use one coordinate equality to deduce the other (example: f(x,y)=(y,3xy), from equality get y equality, then divide by nonzero factor to get x equality). Watch for division by zero and explicitly note nonzero factors when dividing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove surjectivity for functions on product domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an arbitrary target pair in the codomain, explicitly construct input coordinates that map to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solve the system of equations determined by f(x,y)=(u,v) for x,y in terms of u,v (example: f((x,y)) = ((x^2+1)y, x^3): set x = v^{1/3}, y = u/(v^{2/3}+1)). Provide explicit formulas and verify they lie in the domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove set-image inclusions using element-chasing
rubrics_metrics.description: To show inclusions like f(W∩X) ⊆ f(W) ∩ f(X), take an element of the left-hand set and show it belongs to the right-hand set by exhibiting the preimage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical pattern: let b ∈ f(W∩X) so b = f(a) for some a ∈ W∩X; then a ∈ W and a ∈ X so b ∈ f(W) and b ∈ f(X), hence b ∈ f(W)∩f(X). Provide the direct element argument; no need for surjectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove image-of-union equals union-of-images by two inclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove f(W∪X) = f(W) ∪ f(X) show both f(W∪X) ⊆ f(W) ∪ f(X) and f(W) ∪ f(X) ⊆ f(W∪X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First direction: take b ∈ f(W∪X) so b = f(a) with a ∈ W∪X; handle cases a∈W or a∈X to conclude b ∈ f(W) or f(X). Second direction: any b ∈ f(W) ∪ f(X) arises from some a∈W or a∈X and thus from W∪X. Use explicit case analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preimage-of-union equals union-of-preimages
rubrics_metrics.description: For f : A→B and Y,Z ⊆ B, show f^{-1}(Y∪Z) = f^{-1}(Y) ∪ f^{-1}(Z) by proving both subset relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Element-chasing with the definition of preimage: a ∈ f^{-1}(Y∪Z) iff f(a) ∈ Y∪Z, which is equivalent to f(a)∈Y or f(a)∈Z, i.e., a∈f^{-1}(Y) or a∈f^{-1}(Z). Then reverse inclusion similarly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show X ⊆ f^{-1}(f(X)) (always true)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any X ⊆ A, the inclusion X ⊆ f^{-1}(f(X)) holds because every element of X maps into f(X) and hence lies in the preimage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof template: let a∈X ⇒ f(a)∈f(X) ⇒ a∈f^{-1}(f(X)). Note the anti-pattern: equality need not hold in general (counterexamples exist).

rubrics_metrics.name: Epsilon–delta proofs for limits of functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the formal ε–δ definition: given ε>0 produce δ>0 (often depending on ε and c) such that 0<|x−c|<δ implies |f(x)−L|<ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common tactics: factor expressions, use triangle inequality, bound problematic factors by choosing δ ≤ 1 (or other convenient bound) to obtain simpler inequalities. Examples: linear functions use δ=ε/|coefficient|; for x^2 near 3 choose δ ≤1 to bound |x+3| ≤7 and then set δ ≤ ε/7.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit laws and induction for sums
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove the limit of a sum (or finite combination) of functions equals the sum of limits, apply limit laws and induction on the number of summands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base case n=2 follows from sum rule; then assume result for k summands and add the (k+1)-th term using the limit rules. Use constant multiple and identity rules for polynomials, deducing lim_{x→c} f(x)=f(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of limits
rubrics_metrics.description: If lim_{x→c} f(x)=L and lim_{x→c} f(x)=M then L=M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: consider lim of difference equals L−M and also equals 0, so L−M=0. This is the standard contradiction-by-difference technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of compositions with continuous functions
rubrics_metrics.description: If lim_{x→∞} g(x)=L and f is continuous at L, then lim_{x→∞} f(g(x)) = f(L).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use continuity at L to convert an ε for f into a δ for its argument, then use the limit of g to make g(x) within δ of L for large x. Formal ε–δ chaining as in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove nonexistence/divergence of limits via oscillation or undefined points
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that no single limit exists by exhibiting sequences or points approaching the limit point where function values either oscillate or are undefined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: log10|x| as x→0 has values tending to −∞ on sequences approaching 0; x cot(1/x) undefined at 1/(kπ) and thus no limit exists. Use contradiction: assume limit exists and produce points violating ε–δ condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove sequence convergence by choosing N from inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Given ε>0, find N such that n>N implies |a_n−L|<ε by bounding |a_n−L| with expressions involving n and comparing to ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patterns: derive an inequality |a_n−L| ≤ g(n), then choose N so g(n)<ε for n>N (example: 2^n/n! ≤ 4^n/n! and choose N via bounds). Standard technique for rational/power sequences and factorial bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of convergent sequences converges to product
rubrics_metrics.description: If a_n→L and b_n→M then a_n b_n→LM; prove by adding and subtracting LM and applying triangle inequality with bounds on b_n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical estimate: |a_n b_n − LM| ≤ |a_n||b_n−M| + |M||a_n−L|; bound |a_n| by |L|+1 for n large and make each term <ε/2 to get overall <ε. Choose N using convergence of both sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: If |a_n|→0 then a_n→0
rubrics_metrics.description: Convergence of absolute values to 0 implies convergence of the sequence to 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct from definition: |a_n−0| = |a_n|, so any δ/N choice for |a_n| suffices. Example contrasts with case |a_n|→L≠0 where a_n may not converge (sign oscillation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove divergence to infinity implies divergence
rubrics_metrics.description: If a_n→∞ then the sequence does not converge to any finite limit (contradiction via definitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume a_n→L finite and pick ε=1; find N for both convergence assumption and divergence-to-∞ property to obtain contradiction (one gives |a_n−L|<1, the other gives a_n−L>1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard construction of bijections to prove equal cardinalities
rubrics_metrics.description: To show two sets have the same cardinality construct explicit bijections or exhibit injections both ways and appeal to Cantor-Bernstein-Schröder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: e^x maps R→(0,∞); π cot^{-1} maps R→(0,1); map {0,1}×N to N via parity trick f(a,n)=2^n−a; power-set bijections induced by base bijections Φ(X)={f(x):x∈X}. When direct bijection is hard, produce injections both ways and use Cantor-Bernstein.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show countability by explicit listing or bijection with N
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate a set is countably infinite by giving an explicit enumeration or a bijection from N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patterns: list elements in a sequence (e.g., pairs (0,1),(1,1),(0,2),...), produce formulas f(n) for element nth. For sets of finite subsets use prime encoding f({n1,...,nk}) = p_{n1} p_{n2}⋯ to inject into N and list by increasing image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition N into finitely many countably infinite sets via congruence classes
rubrics_metrics.description: For fixed modulus k, partition N into k infinite sets by residues modulo k to produce k countably infinite subsets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define X_i = {n ∈ N : n ≡ i (mod k)} for i=1..k. Each X_i is countably infinite and their union is N.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent subsets/functions equivalently: indicator functions and power set bijection
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a natural bijection between functions N→{0,1} and the power set P(N) via indicator sets: ϕ ↦ {n : ϕ(n)=1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show injectivity and surjectivity by constructing ϕ from any subset X (set ϕ(n)=1 iff n∈X). Use this to relate cardinalities |P(N)| and |{0,1}^N|.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Cantor-Bernstein-Schröder to compare continuum cardinalities
rubrics_metrics.description: To show two uncountable sets have equal cardinality, supply injections both ways and invoke Cantor-Bernstein-Schröder theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in text: to show |B|=|R^2| for B the unit disk, give inclusion map B→R^2 and explicit injection R^2→B (e.g., radial squeezing map g(x,y)=( x/(x^2+y^2+1), y/(x^2+y^2+1) ) ), then apply Cantor-Bernstein.
